claims.text: What the image looks like Saccular/fusiform thoracic aortic dilation >5.5 cm → thoracic aortic aneurysm
claims.quote: Saccular/fusiform thoracic aortic dilation >5.5 cm Thoracic aortic aneurysm

claims.text: Aspects (abnormal in red) Definition: a thoracic aortic diameter ≥ 50% larger than normal (normal diameter varies by location)
claims.quote: A thoracic aortic diameter ≥ 50% larger than normal is considered an aneurysm (normal diameter varies by location).

claims.text: Generally considered large: ascending aorta > 5.5 cm or twice its native size (or aortic size index ≥ 2.75 cm/m2); descending aorta > 6 cm; Marfan syndrome ≥ 4.5 to 5 cm in any location
claims.quote: Aneurysms of the ascending aorta are generally considered large if the diameter is > 5.5 cm or twice the native size of the ascending aorta or if the aortic size index (aortic diameter in relation to body surface area) is ≥ 2.75 cm/m2. In the descending aorta, aneurysms are generally considered large if they are > 6 cm. In patients with Marfan syndrome, large aneurysms are those that are ≥ 4.5 to 5 cm in any location.

claims.text: Rupture risk appears to rise abruptly as TAAs reach 6 cm; median diameter at rupture is about 6 cm (ascending) and 7 cm (descending); smaller aneurysms may also rupture, especially with connective tissue disorders or saccular aneurysms
claims.quote: The risk of rupture appears to rise abruptly as TAAs reach 6 cm in diameter. Median diameter at aneurysm rupture is approximately 6 cm for ascending aneurysms and 7 cm for descending aneurysms (1, 2); smaller aneurysms also may rupture, especially in patients with connective tissue disorders or saccular aneurysms.

claims.text: CXR: often first suspected from an incidental widened mediastinum or enlarged aortic knob, but CXR has poor sensitivity and is not a reliable diagnostic tool
claims.quote: Thoracic aortic aneurysms are usually first suspected when a chest radiograph incidentally shows a widened mediastinum or enlargement of the aortic knob. However, chest radiography has poor sensitivity for TAA and is not a reliable diagnostic tool (eg, in patients with chest pain and suspected aortic aneurysm).

claims.text: Confirmed with CT angiography, MR angiography or transthoracic echocardiography
claims.quote: Diagnosis is often first suspected based on an incidental radiograph or CT finding, and confirmed using CT angiography, magnetic resonance angiography, or transthoracic echocardiography.

claims.text: Causes Most result from atherosclerosis; risk factors include prolonged hypertension, dyslipidemia and smoking, plus aneurysms elsewhere, infection, aortitis and older age (peak 65 to 70 years)
claims.quote: Most thoracic aortic aneurysms result from Atherosclerosis Risk factors for both thoracic aortic aneurysms and aortic dissections include prolonged hypertension, dyslipidemia, and smoking. Additional risk factors for TAAs include presence of aneurysms elsewhere in the body, infection, aortitis, and older age (peak incidence at age 65 to 70 years).

claims.text: Congenital connective tissue disorders (eg, Marfan, Ehlers-Danlos, Loeys-Dietz) cause cystic medial necrosis, leading to TAAs complicated by dissection and by annuloaortic ectasia with aortic regurgitation
claims.quote: Congenital connective tissue disorders (eg, Marfan syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Loeys-Dietz syndrome) cause cystic medial necrosis, a degenerative change that leads to TAAs complicated by aortic dissection and by widening of the proximal aorta and aortic valve (annuloaortic ectasia), which causes aortic regurgitation.

claims.text: Symptoms Most are asymptomatic until complications (thromboembolism, rupture, aortic regurgitation, dissection)
claims.quote: Most thoracic aortic aneurysms are asymptomatic until complications (eg, thromboembolism, rupture, aortic regurgitation, dissection) develop.

claims.text: Compression of adjacent structures: back pain (vertebra), cough or wheezing (tracheobronchial tree), dysphagia (esophagus), hoarseness (left recurrent laryngeal or vagus nerve), chest pain (coronary artery), superior vena cava syndrome
claims.quote: However, compression of adjacent structures can cause back pain (due to compression of vertebra), cough or wheezing (due to compression of the tracheobronchial tree), dysphagia (due to esophageal compression), hoarseness (due to left recurrent laryngeal or vagus nerve compression), chest pain (due to coronary artery compression), and superior vena cava syndrome (due to compression of the central veins or superior vena cava).

claims.text: Erosion into the lungs causes hemoptysis or pneumonitis; into the esophagus (aortoesophageal fistula), massive hematemesis
claims.quote: Erosion of aneurysms into the lungs causes hemoptysis or pneumonitis; erosion into the esophagus (aortoesophageal fistula) causes massive hematemesis.

claims.text: Treatment and next step Her chart: surgical repair (Marfan, bicuspid AV at lower threshold)
claims.quote: Surgical repair (Marfan, bicuspid AV at lower threshold)

claims.text: Larger or symptomatic TAAs: endovascular stent grafting when anatomically possible; open surgical repair for more complex aneurysms
claims.quote: Treat larger or symptomatic TAAs with endovascular stent grafting when anatomically possible and open surgical repair for more complex aneurysms.

claims.text: Asymptomatic aneurysms not meeting repair criteria: aggressive BP control with a beta-blocker (other antihypertensives if needed); smoking cessation is essential; treat dyslipidemia, diabetes and respiratory diseases
claims.quote: Asymptomatic aneurysms that do not meet criteria for elective surgical or endovascular repair are treated with aggressive blood pressure control using a beta-blocker and other antihypertensives if necessary. Smoking cessation is essential. Dyslipidemia, diabetes, and respiratory diseases should all be treated.

claims.text: Follow-up: serial CT or ultrasound every 6 to 12 months, depending on aneurysm size
claims.quote: Patients require frequent follow-ups to check for symptoms and serial CT or ultrasound every 6 to 12 months. Imaging frequency depends on aneurysm size.
